title_content.content: The Increasing Importance of Demand Technicals in Credit

paragraph_content.content: - USD and EUR investment grade (IG) corporate bond markets are on pace for record amounts of primary market supply this year, and issuance in leveraged finance markets remains brisk as well. While there has been meaningful dispersion across sectors and ratings, most index-level spread valuations are hovering towards the tight end of their (post-financial crisis) historical ranges.

In our view, this reflects a generally supportive demand backdrop, at least in aggregate. It also sparks an obvious question: Can this demand tailwind persist? In this Global Credit Trader, we take stock of several measures of credit market demand to address this question.

At a high level, we expect the aggregate demand technical will be an important offset to the heavy pace of supply, which we anticipate will continue across most markets. That said, the concentrated nature of debt issuance within the AI-related ecosystem is likely to push spreads modestly wider per our existing forecasts, with the risks skewed toward more meaningful widening.

Fund flows show very steady demand for USD IG bonds and leveraged loans so far this year, while flows for USD HY and EUR IG and HY have been more muted (but remain positive). Under the surface, there has been a marked preference for passive ETFs and for shorter duration funds, with inflows into longer duration funds lagging since May.

TRACE data also shows strong net demand for corporate bonds in the secondary market but echoes the weakness for longer-duration paper seen in the fund flow data. Recent TIC reports show near-record demand for US domestic corporate bonds from foreign investors. New issue concessions also remain healthy in aggregate, though there have been instances of larger concessions for some recent AI-related financings. Aggregate coupon payments—which have grown to be more sizable following the 2022-2023 rate hiking cycle—also remain an important ‘passive’ demand tailwind, as they are reinvested into the corporate bond market.

title_content.content: The Increasing Importance of Demand Technicals in Credit

paragraph_content.content: The acceleration in new issue activity across the corporate credit market has been closely watched by market participants so far this year. Both the USD and EUR Investment Grade (IG) markets are on pace for new annual gross issuance records, with USD IG issuance approaching $1.5 trillion year to date (up 31% year over year) and EUR IG volumes at €535 billion (up 4% YoY). Leveraged finance supply has also remained steady, albeit shy of record territory. USD HY gross supply at $195 billion is up nearly 10% over last year's pace and EUR HY supply at €70 billion is down 13%.

As a result of the heavy pace of primary market activity, investors have been acutely focused on the demand side of the equation. In this Global Credit Trader we take stock of several measures of credit market demand. At a high level, we expect the aggregate demand technical will be an important offset to the heavy pace of supply, which we anticipate will continue across most markets. That said, the concentrated nature of debt issuance within the AI-related ecosystem is likely to push spreads modestly wider per our existing forecasts, with the risks skewed toward more meaningful widening.

title_content.content: Fund flows: Mostly solid

paragraph_content.content: The most immediate barometer for demand is fund flow data, which provides both real-time and granular insights. According to EPFR, broad USD IG bond ETFs have enjoyed net inflows for 65 consecutive weeks. Exhibit 1 illustrates that USD IG funds have added roughly 8% to their assets under management (AUM) via net inflows this year, while USD bank loan funds (including CLO-focused funds) have added over 6%. The sole laggard has been USD High Yield (HY) funds, which have generated a modest inflow of 0.6% YTD.

paragraph_content.content: In the EUR market, flows have been softer but remain positive. Exhibit 2 highlights YTD cumulative net inflows of 0.4% for pure EUR IG corporate funds and 1.2% for EUR HY funds. While these figures may appear subdued on the surface, it is notable that every major credit market has garnered positive net inflows YTD despite tight valuations and multiple macro headwinds (most prominently, commodity market disruptions from geopolitical conflicts).

Beneath the headline flow data, several structural themes emerge. Exhibit 3 shows cumulative YTD net flows across various vehicles: ETFs (active and passive) and mutual funds. Passive ETFs have dominated YTD flows across most asset classes, while active mutual funds have mostly experienced net outflows. Given the rising dispersion in credit markets, notably around the AI theme, it is likely that investors have migrated to using the ETF wrapper to achieve active manager selection which helps to explain the rise of the smaller, active ETF funds at the expense of mutual funds. The notable exception is in the leveraged loan market, where existing actively managed CLO ETFs have come to dominate loan-related flows over the past few years.

paragraph_content.content: Another important nuance is the recent bifurcation of IG flows across the curve. Exhibit 4 demonstrates that YTD IG corporate fund inflows have been more concentrated in short- and intermediate-duration funds over the last few months, while longer-duration funds have lagged since May (although are still posting inflows). For context, long-duration funds account for 15% of AUM in USD IG corporate funds, with short- and intermediate-duration funds accounting for 36% and 49% of AUM, respectively.

Exhibit 4: Demand for long-end corporate IG bonds has been more tepid than for front-end and intermediate durations

chart_caption.content: Source: EPFR, GS Global Investment Research

paragraph_content.content: While demand from yield-based buyers likely buoyed long duration bonds in the first four months of the year, the demand for long-duration assets has been more tepid as of late. This is likely a dual response to (1) a supply headwind at the long-end of the curve and (2) some residual uncertainty among credit investors related to the path of long-end rates, given the Fed leadership transition and potential changes in the central bank's reaction function and approach to areas such as the balance sheet. Year-to-date performance also reflects this weakness. USD IG front-end spreads have tightened by 5bp YTD, while spreads on the 25+ year maturity index have widened by 15bp.

title_content.content: 'Dealer lift' volumes reveal an investor preference for shorter maturities

paragraph_content.content: Another robust metric of corporate credit demand is trade-level data, specifically the “net dealer lift” amount, which measures dealer-to-customer trades reported in TRACE, netting customer buys against customer sells. Aggregate data for both the USD IG and HY bond markets reveals a healthy appetite for corporate bonds, with the IG market on track for record net buying and the HY market pacing for its second-highest year on record after 2020 (Exhibit 5).

Zooming in on the net dealer lift data across the curve corroborates the fund flow narrative: net demand for long-end bonds has underperformed relative to the front end and belly. For instance, bonds with maturities greater than 12 years have accounted for 26% of YTD total trading volumes but account for just 22% of YTD net demand. Conversely, IG bonds with a maturity between 3 and 7 years have represented 27% of aggregate trading volumes this year but have accounted for an outsized 49% of net customer demand.

title_content.content: Other measures of demand also point to a solid backdrop

paragraph_content.content: To complete our review of corporate bond demand, we look at three additional metrics: foreign net purchases of US bonds, new issue concessions, and passive demand from recycled coupon payments. All three point to a supportive backdrop.

Exhibit 6 shows a 3-month average of net purchases of US corporate bonds using the Treasury TIC data. (Note: this data references the residence of the issuer, not the currency of the bond.) The key takeaway is that foreign demand (with a caveat that the data is lagged by six weeks) has currently reached new post-financial crisis highs. In fact, the top five highest monthly totals for net foreign demand since the end of the financial crisis have all come in the last 18-months. As of May 2026, net long-term purchases by foreign investors totaled $439 billion over the trailing 12-month period, pushing total foreign holdings to a record $5.3 trillion. Looking below the surface, about half of the foreign demand so far this year has originated from Europe, with the rest spread across other regions.

paragraph_content.content: Second, we monitor new issue concessions to gauge the market's digestion of incremental supply. Despite recent anecdotes of a few large AI-related deals pricing with higher-than-typical concessions, the aggregate data paints a more benign picture—at least so far. Exhibit 7 tracks the 4-week moving average of our estimate of new issue concessions for the USD and EUR IG markets. While both markets experienced upward pressure during the early stages of the Middle East conflict, they have since restabilized in the low- to mid-single digits—a range consistent with the past decade. Given our expectations for additional debt issuance from the AI-related ecosystem, we will be monitoring this metric closely.

chart_footnote.content: Source: iBoxx, Dealogic, GS Global Investment Research

paragraph_content.content: Finally, we view coupon payments as a powerful source of passive demand, operating under the assumption that the majority of these payments are recycled back into the corporate bond market. Exhibits 8 and 9 plot our estimates of annual coupon payments against net supply in the USD and EUR IG and HY markets. Despite accelerating net supply this year, aggregate coupon payments have also grown, driven by higher all-in yields resulting from the 2022-2023 rate hiking cycle. We estimate that coupon payments alone will absorb more than 50% of net supply in the USD IG and HY markets (Exhibit 8) and roughly 40% of net supply in the EUR IG and HY markets (Exhibit 9). While lower than the percentages seen over the last few years, this remains very healthy compared to the past decade.

paragraph_content.content: None of these demand measures is comprehensive on its own—each has its flaws and potential blind spots. That said, this broad array of metrics points to a supportive aggregate demand technical. We expect this will be an important mitigant to the heavy pace of supply that we expect.

That said, the concentrated nature of debt issuance within the AI-related ecosystem is likely to push spreads modestly wider per our existing forecasts, with the risks skewed toward more meaningful widening.

table_footnote.content: Source: GS Global Investment Research

content.html:
Relative value views
Corporate Credit
RegionalOverweight USD vs. EURThe growth, inflation and monetary policy mix is somewhat more favorable in the US, relative to Europe. As a result, and relative to the USD market, we forecast a wider peak (and a slower recovery in 2H2026) in EUR credit spreads.
Overweight EUR IG CLO tranches vs. USD IG CLO tranchesEUR IG tranches offer carry pickup relative to USD IG CLO tranches. While the policy and macroeconomic picture is less supportive in Europe, subordination should protect tranches up in the capital structure from a continued idiosyncratic default picture.
USD marketOverweight IG vs. HYWe have a slight preference for IG vs. HY in the USD market, owing to valuations and our economists' forecasts for below-potential growth. We view the BB/BBB spread ratio as fairly priced amid a somewhat more challenging growth and inflation mix, and have a neutral view between the two rating cohorts.
Overweight BBBs vs. higher-rated cohortsWe prefer owning BBBs over the higher-rated segments of USD IG (As and AAs), as a way to capture additional spread. We also see scope for balance sheet deterioration at the highest end of the rating spectrum in IG.
Overweight BBs, Neutral CCCs, Underweight BsCurrent spread levels indicate that single-Bs offer the lowest credit risk premium relative to expected losses among all HY rating buckets.
Overweight HY bonds vs. loansHY bonds still provide a superior trade-off between carry and duration compared to leveraged loans. In addition, loans' substantial software sector exposure is likely to present a sentiment overhang, at least in the near-term.
Overweight CLO mezz tranches vs. leveraged loansNeutral CLO vs. USD IGNeutral CLO vs. CMOsFor floating rate investors, we prefer CLO mezzanine tranches vs. leveraged loans. Historical data points to low impairment rates for BB and BBB CLO tranches, and current valuations offer attractive carry and a cushion against moderate to elevated default outcomes. Elsewhere, we are neutral between senior CLO tranches and USD IG; we would use spread widening to add exposure in CLOs. We are also neutral between CLO AAA and CMO floaters.
Prefer Agency MBS vs. IGAgency MBS offers an attractive diversification benefit vs. a portfolio of IG corporate bonds.
Overweight Hybrids vs. BBBsWe view the additional spread compensation of hybrids vs. BBBs as moderately attractive in the context of the tight spread environment. We also expect the hybrid spread premium to compress vs. BBBs, as the hybrid market grows further.
EUR marketOverweight IG vs. HYWe prefer IG over HY given the more challenging growth, inflation, and monetary policy mix in the Euro Area.
Overweight As vs. BBBsIn the EUR market, we prefer As over BBBs, as the weaker growth backdrop warrants more of an up-in-quality stance. That said, we would not move too far up the quality spectrum, as we expect supply technicals will be a headwind in the EUR AA market.
Overweight HY bonds vs. loansSimilar to the US, we prefer HY bonds given the loan market's weighting toward software (and the potential negative sentiment overhang). The reaction function of the ECB may also increase borrowing costs for floating rate issuers, given the central bank's focus on inflationary pressures.
Overweight BBs, Neutral Bs, Underweight CCCsAt current valuations and given our expectation for heightened dispersion, we prefer moving up in quality within EUR HY.
